items.title: Endogenous shareholding auctions
items.abstract: We introduce endogenous shareholding auctions for production economies where a monopolist must elicit consumer demand in order to determine price and quantity. Each of these auctions has the property that the auction's profit is distributed across the monopolist and the consumers in accordance with ownership shares that are determined over the course of the auction. We characterize this class, and a larger class, on the basis of standard axioms. Finally, we investigate optimal auctions according to both prior-free domination and subjective expected welfare.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new type of auction model called 'endogenous shareholding auctions,' where a monopolist (a single seller) must gather consumer demand data to set prices and quantities. The auction distributes profits between the monopolist and consumers based on ownership shares that emerge during the auction process. The authors analyze these auctions using standard economic principles and explore optimal auction designs from both fairness and efficiency perspectives.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on theoretical auction design, its exploration of monopolistic pricing and consumer demand elicitation could indirectly inform debates about digital platforms' market power and pricing strategies.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals the importance of understanding how digital platforms (monopolists) extract consumer data to set prices, highlighting potential concerns about fairness and consumer welfare in digital markets.

items.title: Washed Out by the Crowd? Accountability under Sequential Review
items.abstract: When an early information producer is judged only after others have reviewed and revised the work, the same review that sharpens the final decision can blur the question of who deserves the credit. This paper asks how an organization can still reward careful early work once a chain of later reviewers has acted on it. In the model, an analyst's hidden effort makes an initial report more likely to be right; a sequence of reviewers then reacts to it; and the organization can pay only on the record this process leaves behind. The main result splits the value of any such record into two parts: how much effort improved the first report, and how well the final record still indicates whether the first report was accurate. When later reviewers can overturn a flawed report, review improves decisions but washes the analyst's effort out of the final outcome; therefore, rewarding the final outcome stops working, while rewarding agreement between the first and last word has incentive value instead. When the first report is simply copied by downstream reviewers, the reverse holds. Which reward is better comes down to one thing: how likely the review process is to repair an initial mistake.

_analysis.summary: This paper explores how organizations can fairly reward early contributors (like analysts) when their work is later reviewed and revised by others. It models a process where an initial report’s quality depends on hidden effort, but the final outcome is shaped by subsequent reviewers, making it hard to credit the original work. The study splits the value of the final record into parts to assess contributions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Relevant for digital competition because it highlights how sequential review processes (e.g., in platform content moderation or AI model training) can obscure accountability, affecting incentives for innovation and compliance in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that sequential review and revision in digital ecosystems (e.g., AI training pipelines, platform content moderation) may create accountability gaps, potentially distorting competitive dynamics.

items.title: Congestion-Based Slot Pricing in a Railway Auction Game
items.abstract: We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback. We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively trig

_analysis.summary: This paper models how multiple competing agents (e.g., railway operators) bid for scarce, congested resources (e.g., train slots) using an auction system that adjusts prices based on demand and individual behavior. The system penalizes the largest bidder and rewards the smallest to balance usage, which could reduce congestion and improve efficiency.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how auction mechanisms with congestion-based pricing and asymmetric adjustments can shape resource allocation among competing agents, offering insights for digital platform regulation where scarce resources (e.g., ad slots, API access) are allocated.
_analysis.market_signal: Auction-based resource allocation with behavioral adjustments could inspire new models for regulating digital platforms' access to critical infrastructure or data, akin to railway slot management.

items.title: Decomposing Wage Stagnation: Employment Reallocation, Wage Structure,and Demographics
items.abstract: Average wages in Japan rose until the mid-1990s but stagnated thereafter. This paper studies Japan's long-run wage stagnation by decomposing changes in average log real hourly wages from 1980 to 2024 into four components: demographic change across worker types, changes in relative employment shares across job types, changes in relative wages across job types, and wage growth within job types. The framework combines a shift-share decomposition across worker types with an extension of the Olley-Pakes decomposition that separates employment reallocation from changes in relative wages across job types. Wage growth within job types contributes positively over the full sample period, but demographic change and employment reallocation partly offset it. Between 1996 and 2014, all four components are negative. The negative contribution from employment reallocation is not limited to the expansion of part-time employment, but reflects broader shifts across job types defined by employment type, establishment size, and industry.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines Japan's wage stagnation since the mid-1990s by breaking down average wage changes into four parts: shifts in worker demographics, changes in employment across job types, wage differences between job types, and wage growth within the same job. Using a method that combines demographic analysis with employment reallocation (the Olley-Pakes decomposition), it shows how these factors interact to explain stagnant wages over time.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on wage stagnation in Japan's labor market rather than digital markets, its methodology for decomposing structural changes could be adapted to analyze shifts in digital labor markets or platform employment dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the importance of decomposing structural shifts in labor markets, which may inspire similar analyses for digital labor platforms or AI-driven employment changes.

items.title: Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
items.abstract: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, they increasingly ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface: a misaligned or prompt-injected agent can distribute attacks across pull requests (PRs) and time its payload for the PR with the best natural cover. To study the resulting dynamics, we introduce Iterative VibeCoding, a setting for AI control, the study of safely deploying capable but potentially untrusted AI. In Iterative VibeCoding, a coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Our benchmark includes two task families: CLI tools and Flask web services, across 20 total task variations. We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the attack agent and GPT-4o as the monitor. We compare gradual attacks, which distribute the side task across PRs, against non-gradual attacks concentrated in a single PR. No single monitor is robust to both: which strategy evades best (success while evading the monitor) depends on the monitor type, so a defender cannot close off both gradual and non-gradual attacks with any one monitor. High evasion (>= 65%) generalizes across mod

_analysis.summary: This paper warns that increasingly autonomous AI coding agents could be misused to distribute harmful code over time through multiple software updates (called 'pull requests' or PRs), making attacks harder to detect. It introduces a new framework called 'Iterative VibeCoding' to study how to safely deploy untrusted AI in software development while minimizing risks like prompt injection attacks.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights a new vector for AI-driven market disruption where autonomous agents could subtly alter software ecosystems, potentially creating competitive advantages for firms controlling these agents or exposing vulnerabilities in digital infrastructure.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals the rise of autonomous AI agents in software development that could reshape competitive dynamics in tech markets by enabling stealthy, distributed attacks or manipulations.

items.title: LACUNA: A Testbed for Evaluating Localization Precision for LLM Unlearning
items.abstract: LLMs memorize sensitive training data, including personally identifiable information (PII), creating a pressing need for reliable post hoc removal methods. Unlearning has emerged as a promising solution, with state-of-the-art(SOTA) methods often following a localize-first, unlearn-second paradigm that targets specific model parameters. However, existing benchmarks evaluate unlearning solely at the output level, leaving open the question of whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from a model's parameters or merely obfuscates it, a concern reinforced by the success of resurfacing attacks. To bridge this gap, we introduce LACUNA: the first unlearning testbed with ground-truth parameter-level localization. LACUNA injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining, enabling direct evaluation of whether unlearning targets the weights responsible for knowledge storage. We use LACUNA to benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and find that, despite strong output-level performance, existing methods are highly imprecise and susceptible to resurfacing attacks. We further show that when localization is successful

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces LACUNA, a new benchmark for testing how well large language models (LLMs) can forget specific information, like personal details, when asked to 'unlearn' it. Current methods often only hide the information in the model's outputs, but the paper warns that attackers can still retrieve the forgotten data, raising concerns about whether unlearning truly removes knowledge or just disguises it.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights a critical flaw in AI 'unlearning' techniques that could undermine trust in AI systems, potentially affecting competition in AI-driven markets where data privacy and reliability are key differentiators.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that current AI unlearning methods may not be robust enough for real-world deployment, which could delay adoption of AI systems in regulated industries and impact competition.

items.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
items.abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces 'Program-as-Weights' (PAW), a new way to turn natural-language instructions into compact, locally-run neural networks. Instead of relying on large language model APIs—which can be slow, expensive, and hard to reproduce—PAW compiles these functions into smaller, reusable models that work offline.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: PAW demonstrates how AI can replace cloud-based API calls with local models, potentially reducing dependence on dominant AI service providers and reshaping competition in AI infrastructure markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Local AI model compilation could erode the dominance of cloud-based AI providers like Microsoft Azure or AWS, shifting power to firms that can train or fine-tune smaller models efficiently.

items.title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
items.abstract: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how to monitor large language models (LLMs) in real time to detect unsafe outputs, even after alignment training. It proposes a simple threshold-based alarm system that flags outputs when safety risks exceed a calibrated limit, showing this approach works as well as more complex methods in tests on math reasoning and red teaming datasets.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights the need for robust safety monitoring in AI systems, which could become a regulatory obligation under AI risk frameworks, potentially reshaping compliance costs and competitive barriers for AI developers.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing reliance on third-party safety monitors and risk calibration tools, which may become a competitive advantage for firms with proprietary monitoring systems.

items.title: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
items.abstract: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications. Although recent LLMs support increasingly long context windows, they often fail to use relevant evidence that is already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning (RECONTEXT), a training-free inference method for improving long-context reasoning. RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals to construct a query-conditioned evidence pool and replays it before final generation while preserving the full original context. This recursive selection process separates evidence organization from answer generation without training, external memory, or context pruning. We also provide a theoretical analysis based on associative memory, which characterizes the context as a memory store, the question as a retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation. Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length show that RECONTEXT consistently improves evidenc

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces RECONTEXT (Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning), a new method to improve how large language models (LLMs) process and reason over long documents. The technique helps LLMs better identify and use relevant evidence within their input, addressing a gap where models struggle to utilize context effectively despite having access to it.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how advancements in LLM reasoning could reduce the competitive moats of dominant AI platforms by improving their ability to process and synthesize information, potentially enabling new entrants to compete more effectively.
_analysis.market_signal: Improved long-context reasoning in LLMs may accelerate the development of AI-powered tools that can challenge incumbents in markets like search, legal research, or enterprise software by offering more accurate and efficient analysis.

items.title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
items.abstract: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. W

_analysis.summary: This study examines how large language model (LLM) agents behave differently when their responses are public versus private (off-the-record, OTR) in structured debates. It finds that social context—such as audience and role—shapes what agents choose to express publicly, even without explicit instructions. This suggests that LLMs may adapt their behavior based on perceived expectations or strategic considerations in multi-agent interactions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates that AI agents can strategically alter their public behavior based on social context, signaling potential for manipulation or coordination in digital markets where such agents interact.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents may develop latent objectives that prioritize perceived social or strategic advantages over factual accuracy, raising concerns about transparency and fairness in digital ecosystems.

items.title: DemoPSD: Disagreement-Modulated Policy Self-Distillation
items.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a practical method for training large language models (LLMs) to reason, where a single model acts as both the teacher and the student with different levels of information access. However, recent studies have found that the teacher's dense token-level supervision, conditioned on privileged information, can lead to overfitting to in-domain patterns, suppress exploration, and hurt cross-domain generalization, while also introducing a more fundamental issue: *privileged information leakage*, where the student encodes answer-dependent shortcuts that are unavailable at test time. We introduce **DemoPSD**, a novel framework that resolves such problems through the idea of *selective adoption of teacher guidance*. Instead of fitting the full teacher distribution, DemoPSD steers the student toward a *reverse-KL barycenter target*, a weighted geometric combination of the teacher and student distributions, that naturally balances learning from the teacher with preserving the student's own reasoning capacity. We measure the difference between their distributions and use such a discrepancy to adaptively control the blending at each token position

_analysis.summary: This paper examines *on-policy self-distillation (OPSD)*, a method for training large language models (LLMs) where the same model acts as both teacher and student. It finds that using privileged information (extra data the student doesn’t have) can cause the model to overfit to specific patterns, reduce its ability to generalize, and create *privileged information leakage*, where the model relies on shortcuts that depend on the answer rather than the input.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals how AI training methods can inadvertently reinforce market power by making models dependent on privileged data, which could entrench dominant platforms that control such data.
_analysis.market_signal: AI training techniques may deepen the advantage of firms with access to large proprietary datasets, potentially exacerbating concentration in AI-driven markets.

items.title: Controllable Sim Agents with Behavior Latents
items.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that imitate logged behavior and can also be steered along interpretable axes. Such controllability enables engineers to isolate variables, reproduce specific edge cases, and test autonomous systems without real-world risk. We introduce Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable simulated-agent framework that learns to infer a per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update, conditioning a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. To tackle scarcity in reward signals, we propose soft eligibility gates that replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay, preserving the gradient signal for near-threshold agents. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA attains competitive realism on the benchmark while exposing per-channel controllability that the higher-ranked imitation models lack. Speed- and acceleration-based steering produces monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with the introduction of soft eligib

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a framework for creating AI-driven simulated agents that can mimic real-world behavior while being steered along specific, interpretable paths. These agents use a technique called 'behavior latents' (hidden variables representing agent actions) and a 'rectified-flow trajectory generator' (a model generating controlled agent movements) to enable precise testing of autonomous systems, such as self-driving cars, without real-world risks.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology signals a shift toward AI-driven simulation tools that could reduce reliance on real-world testing, potentially disrupting traditional market structures in sectors like autonomous vehicles or robotics by lowering barriers to entry for new competitors.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered simulation agents may accelerate innovation in autonomous systems by enabling cheaper, safer testing, potentially challenging incumbent firms' dominance in high-stakes markets like automotive or logistics.

items.title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
items.abstract: Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite. We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a mo

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces TestEvo-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating how software tests and code evolve together in real-world projects. It highlights flaws in existing benchmarks that treat tests and code changes in isolation, making it hard to assess whether automated tools understand how code changes should update tests.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper focuses on software development practices, it indirectly signals the growing complexity of AI-driven software ecosystems, which could impact competition in digital markets where automated testing tools are increasingly used by large tech platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of AI-powered code and test co-evolution tools may reduce barriers to entry for smaller firms competing in software markets, potentially disrupting incumbents' dominance in developer tooling.

items.title: Neuron-Aware Data Selection for Annotation-Free LLM Self-Distillation
items.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) without real-world interaction feedback or human-labeled supervision remains challenging, particularly in specialized domains where expert annotations are costly to obtain. Recent annotation-free self-evolution methods address this by using the model's own outputs as supervision signals, constructing a teacher via additional context and aggregating predictions across multiple rollouts through majority voting to produce pseudo-labels. However, these approaches are not without drawbacks: SFT- and GRPO-based variants suffer out-of-domain performance degradation, while reward-based on-policy RL inflates calibration error. In this paper, we propose Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation (Neuron-OPSD), a data-centric framework for annotation-free self-distillation that leverages internal neuron activations to guide both training-data selection and teacher context construction. The model is then trained via on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution, requiring no ground-truth labels at any stage. Across specialized-domain benchmarks, Neuron-OPSD improves in-domain task performance while preserving cross-domain generalization and mitigating

_analysis.summary: This paper explores ways to improve large language models (LLMs) without relying on expensive human-labeled data or real-world feedback. It proposes methods like self-distillation, where the model uses its own outputs to teach itself, but notes challenges like performance degradation when moving to new domains. The work focuses on technical efficiency rather than market competition.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper advances LLM training techniques, it does not directly address competition policy issues like market power or regulatory obligations.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals ongoing advancements in AI efficiency that could reduce barriers to entry for smaller firms competing with dominant LLM providers.

items.title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
items.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new benchmark called EvoPolicyGym to evaluate how autonomous AI agents can iteratively improve executable policies (sets of rules for decision-making) in interactive environments, such as reinforcement learning (RL) tasks. The authors propose a controlled setting where an AI agent repeatedly edits a policy under a fixed budget, simulating how AI systems might autonomously refine their own performance over time.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals a shift toward AI systems that can autonomously optimize their own policies, which could disrupt traditional market dynamics by enabling rapid, self-driven innovation that outpaces regulated or human-managed competition.
_analysis.market_signal: Autonomous AI policy evolution could accelerate competitive dynamics in digital markets by enabling firms to rapidly iterate and improve their algorithms without human intervention, potentially reducing barriers to entry and intensifying rivalry.

items.title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
items.abstract: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect

_analysis.summary: This study tested whether giving AI coding assistants more tools (like browser-based testing) or design-focused prompts improves their ability to reliably generate software. It found that higher reasoning effort (how hard the AI thinks before acting) was more important for first-try success than extra tools, with 90 independent runs of an AI agent building the same app scored on 14 functional and visual criteria.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows that AI agent capabilities (like reasoning effort) may shift competitive advantages in software development markets, potentially reducing reliance on dominant platforms or tools.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with strong reasoning skills could disrupt traditional software development markets by reducing dependence on proprietary tools or platforms.

items.title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
items.abstract: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). _analysis.summary: This paper tests whether advanced AI models like GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM can grade Linux/bash command-line exam responses as accurately as human experts. It uses a four-level cognitive taxonomy to assess AI's ability to handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, and syntactic variations in grading.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on education, the paper highlights AI's potential to automate complex, nuanced tasks (e.g., grading), signaling broader implications for AI-driven labor market disruption and platform competition in digital services.
_analysis.market_signal: AI's expanding capability to perform specialized, expert-level tasks (like grading) may accelerate automation in digital markets, reducing reliance on human labor and increasing competition among AI service providers.

items.title: QFedAgent: Quantum-Enhanced Personalized Federated Learning for Multi-Agent Activity Recognition
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without sharing raw data, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive robotic sensing applications. However, multi-agent systems generate heterogeneous and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) multimodal sensor streams that degrade conventional FL algorithms, while classical fusion modules introduce substantial parameter overhead and communication cost. This paper proposes QFedAgent, a hybrid quantum-classical personalized FL framework for multi-agent activity recognition. The approach integrates a variational quantum circuit fusion module that models accelerometer--gyroscope interactions through quantum state encoding and entanglement, requiring only 72 quantum rotation parameters versus 33K in classical multi-layer perceptron-based fusion, achieving approximately 10x total parameter reduction. Experiments on the OPPORTUNITY dataset under subject-based non-IID partitions demonstrate 97.7% mean test accuracy, confirming that parameter-efficient quantum fusion remains competitive with conventional federated baselines.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces QFedAgent, a new hybrid quantum-classical federated learning (FL) framework designed to improve multi-agent activity recognition in privacy-sensitive robotic systems. FL allows multiple devices to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data, but struggles with heterogeneous (non-IID) sensor data, which QFedAgent aims to solve using quantum-enhanced techniques.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, QFedAgent highlights the growing role of quantum computing in AI, which could disrupt data aggregation and model training dynamics in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Quantum-enhanced federated learning may accelerate the shift toward decentralized AI training, reducing reliance on large centralized data platforms.

items.title: Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning for LLMs
items.abstract: Active Few-Shot Learning (AFSL) adapts LLMs to specialized domains by identifying the most valuable unlabeled samples for annotation and use as few-shot demonstrations, effectively reducing human annotation costs while promoting high performance. However, existing methods typically rely on output-level signals for sample identification, such as predictive entropy or semantic similarities with test-time data based on external embeddings, which often overlook models' internal dynamics, which could pinpoint specific knowledge gaps. To bridge this gap, we propose NeuFS, a Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning framework that shifts the selection paradigm from output-level proxies to models' internal dynamics. NeuFS utilizes neuron activation patterns to represent sample directly, and includes a dual-criteria selection strategy that: (1) ensures few-shot sample diversity with neuron patterns for broader example coverage, while (2) prioritizing on identifying informative and challenging few-shot samples LLMs tend to hallucinate by quantifying neuron consensus. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that NeuFS excels in both reasoning and text classification tasks, outperforming existin

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces NeuFS, a new method for Active Few-Shot Learning (AFSL) that improves how large language models (LLMs) are fine-tuned for specialized tasks by focusing on the model's internal workings (neurons) rather than just its outputs. AFSL aims to reduce the cost of labeling data by selecting the most useful samples for training, and this approach could make it easier for smaller firms to compete with larger ones that have more training data.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a shift in how AI models are trained, which could lower barriers to entry for smaller firms in AI-driven markets by reducing reliance on large datasets controlled by dominant platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: Neuro-aware training methods like NeuFS could democratize access to high-performance AI models, potentially disrupting the competitive advantage of firms with proprietary datasets.

items.title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Lay

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces SPG-Layout, a new AI framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate 3D indoor scenes in complex, non-Manhattan environments (spaces without straight, right-angled layouts). Unlike existing methods that struggle with non-orthogonal layouts, SPG-Layout improves physical plausibility by modeling spatial relationships more accurately.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper focuses on 3D scene synthesis, it highlights advancements in AI that could indirectly influence digital markets by improving spatial computing applications, which may become relevant for competition in emerging tech sectors like AR/VR or digital twins.
_analysis.market_signal: Advancements in AI-driven 3D scene generation signal growing capabilities in spatial computing, which could disrupt markets for digital design tools, gaming engines, or metaverse platforms.

items.title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
items.abstract: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper introduces a method called RFM-AGOP to efficiently identify multi-dimensional subspaces in Large Language Models (LLMs) that control behaviors like refusing harmful queries. Unlike older methods that are slow and impractical for long reasoning traces, this approach uses the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm to speed up the process.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights the growing complexity of AI model control mechanisms, which could influence how regulators assess the market power of AI-driven platforms and their ability to enforce safety or compliance rules.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in AI interpretability tools may reduce barriers to entry for competitors by enabling more transparent and controllable AI systems, potentially disrupting the dominance of large AI model providers.

items.title: WattGPU: Predicting Inference Power and Latency on Unseen GPUs and LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference workloads are a rapidly growing contributor to data center energy consumption. Optimizing these deployments requires matching specific LLMs to the most efficient GPUs, but operators currently lack the tools to do so without exhaustively profiling each combination. While some predictive models exist, they still require profiling data and struggle to generalize to hardware unseen during training. To address this, we introduce \textit{WattGPU}, featuring two predictive models for mean GPU power draw and Inter-Token Latency (ITL). Our approach leverages only publicly available LLM metadata and GPU specifications, eliminating the need for hardware access or profiling while enabling generalization to unseen NVIDIA server-grade GPUs and LLMs. We evaluate our models using rigorous leave-one-GPU-out and leave-one-LLM-out cross-validation on a dataset of 42 open-source LLMs (0.1B--27B parameters) and 8 GPUs under both offline and server scenarios. The mean power draw model achieves a median absolute percentage error of $\leq3.4\%$ for offline and $\leq13.5\%$ for server scenarios on unseen GPUs, while the latency model achieves $\leq8.5\%$ in server mode,

_analysis.summary: WattGPU is a new tool that predicts how much power and how fast a specific graphics processing unit (GPU) will run a large language model (LLM) without needing to test every possible combination. It helps data center operators choose the most efficient GPUs for LLM tasks, saving energy and costs.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals how hardware efficiency in AI workloads can create competitive advantages for companies with better GPU optimization, potentially reshaping the market for AI infrastructure services.
_analysis.market_signal: The ability to predict GPU performance for LLMs signals a shift toward hardware-software co-design as a key competitive lever in the AI infrastructure market.

items.title: DecompRL: Solving Harder Problems by Learning Modular Code Generation
items.abstract: How can Large Language Models (LLMs) solve problems they currently cannot? Repeated sampling scales test-time compute but GPU cost grows linearly with attempts, while reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards improves single-attempt accuracy at the expense of sample diversity. Both strategies ultimately fail when the base policy has near-zero probability of producing a correct solution: no amount of sampling or gradient signal can overcome a search space that is simply too large. We take a different approach: rather than sampling harder, we make the task easier by decomposing problems into smaller, independently solvable sub-functions whose implementations can be recombined. Since off-the-shelf models are not trained for this modular generation, we introduce DecompRL, an RL algorithm that explicitly learns to decompose and implement hierarchical code structures. Recombining $k$ implementations of $n$ modules yields up to $k^{n}$ candidate solutions, shifting the bottleneck from GPU inference to cheap CPU evaluation and cutting GPU token cost by $\sim$50$\times$. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests (Qwen~2.5~7B, Code World Model~32B), DecompRL outperforms standard and divers

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a method called DecompRL to help Large Language Models (LLMs) solve complex problems by breaking them into smaller, more manageable sub-tasks. Traditional approaches like repeated sampling or reinforcement learning struggle when the base model has almost no chance of producing a correct solution, but this modular approach aims to make tasks easier by decomposing them.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a potential shift in how AI systems could evolve to challenge dominant platforms by improving problem-solving capabilities, which may disrupt market power structures where incumbents rely on proprietary or hard-to-replicate solutions.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems that can decompose and solve complex problems more efficiently may reduce barriers to entry for competitors in digital markets currently dominated by a few gatekeepers.

items.title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
items.abstract: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that coding agents (AI systems that write or modify software) need strict controls like access restrictions and coding conventions to prevent security risks and maintain codebase scalability. It proposes a system where a small AI reviewer enforces these constraints, making human oversight cheaper and more efficient.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI agents could disrupt traditional software development markets by reducing reliance on human oversight, potentially shifting power toward firms controlling these agents.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven coding tools may reduce barriers to entry in software markets, challenging incumbents like Microsoft or GitHub.

items.title: Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
items.abstract: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search system, deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, that takes a natural-language research query and returns the matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR by over 5x. On top of this supervised pipeline, we add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage that, without any additional training, lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces an AI-powered search system for NASA's Earth observation datasets, using large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs (structured databases) to help researchers find relevant data more easily. It demonstrates how agentic search (AI systems that autonomously perform tasks) can unlock hidden value in existing data resources.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows how AI-driven search agents can disrupt traditional data discovery methods, potentially challenging dominant platforms' control over data access and search markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Agentic search systems may reduce reliance on proprietary search engines, threatening gatekeepers' data access dominance in specialized markets like geoscience.

items.title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
items.abstract: Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential. Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management. In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing tem

_analysis.summary: This paper explores how increasingly complex autonomous systems—combining large language models, optimization engines, and real-time hardware—require strict, hardware-enforced coordination to ensure safety and reliability. Current software-based coordination methods fail in high-stakes environments where latency, determinism, and fault tolerance are critical.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights the technical barriers to entry for safety-critical autonomous systems, which could reinforce dominance by firms with deep hardware-software integration capabilities.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals a shift toward vertically integrated, hardware-software stacks in autonomous systems, potentially favoring incumbents like NVIDIA or Tesla over smaller AI startups.

items.title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
items.abstract: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capab

_analysis.summary: This paper explores how personalized language models (LLMs) can change not just their answers but also the *reasoning process* behind those answers when they remember past interactions with a user. The authors introduce DRIFTLENS, a tool to measure how a model’s 'memory' of a user’s preferences or history shifts its internal reasoning steps—even when no single correct answer exists. This could affect how users trust or rely on AI systems in markets where personalized recommendations or advice drive engagement.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows how personalized AI systems (like chatbots or recommendation engines) can subtly alter reasoning trajectories, which may influence consumer behavior and market competition in digital platforms where trust and consistency are key differentiators.
_analysis.market_signal: Personalized AI reasoning drift could erode trust in dominant platforms' AI tools or create opportunities for niche competitors offering more transparent or consistent AI interactions.

items.title: VisionAId: An Offline-First Multimodal Android Assistant for People with Visual Impairment, Featuring Personalized Object Retrieval
items.abstract: Over 285 million people worldwide live with a visual impairment, for whom everyday tasks such as avoiding obstacles, locating personal belongings, recognizing familiar faces, or handling cash remain persistent obstacles to personal autonomy. Existing assistive applications are typically limited to recognizing predefined categories, depend heavily on cloud connectivity, or require dedicated hardware. We present VisionAId, an Android application that turns a commodity smartphone into a real-time visual assistant. The system integrates six on-device deep learning models (metric monocular depth estimation, instance segmentation, visual and facial embeddings, face detection, and a custom banknote detector) running entirely through ONNX Runtime, with an optional cloud large language model (Google Gemini Flash) used only for narrative scene description and automatic object labeling. A distinctive contribution is a few-shot pipeline for personal objects: the user photographs an object from several angles, and the system later locates that specific instance in the environment, guiding the user toward it with augmented-reality markers, spatial audio, and distance-proportional haptics. All fe

_analysis.summary: VisionAId is an Android app that uses on-device AI to help people with visual impairments perform everyday tasks like finding objects or recognizing faces without relying on cloud services. It combines six deep learning models to work offline, addressing limitations of existing cloud-dependent assistive tools.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how on-device AI can reduce dependence on cloud-based platforms, signaling potential shifts in data processing markets and platform power dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: On-device AI assistants may reduce reliance on cloud-dependent services, challenging the dominance of cloud providers and smartphone OS gatekeepers.

items.title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
items.abstract: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

_analysis.summary: This paper studies how AI agents can automatically fix missed optimizations in compilers (software that translates code into efficient machine instructions). It finds that agents struggle to generalize fixes beyond specific cases, unlike human developers. The authors compare AI-generated patches to those made by humans using real-world compiler issues from LLVM (a popular open-source compiler).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, it highlights the growing role of AI in software development, which could impact market dynamics for tech platforms reliant on compiler technologies.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven automation in software development may reduce barriers to entry for competing platforms by lowering reliance on human expertise in critical infrastructure like compilers.

items.title: World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI
items.abstract: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) represent a new form of automated, monolingual cultural interaction and that literary disciplines—such as comparative literature, narratology, and translation—can help build more culturally aware AI systems. It proposes a framework for developing textual models that account for pluralistic interpretations, bridging critical theory with AI development.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, it highlights how LLMs shape cultural markets and may influence platform power by enabling more nuanced AI-driven content interactions.
_analysis.market_signal: LLMs are becoming central to cultural and content markets, potentially shifting competitive dynamics in digital advertising, search, and content moderation.

items.title: The Dual Nature of LLM Persona: Aggregated Tendencies and Frame-Dependent Geometry
items.abstract: Evaluations of LLM personas via psychometric questionnaires typically rely on aggregate scores, discarding within-instance correlation structure. We test whether this geometric structure is intrinsic or frame-dependent. Constructing within-instance correlation matrices from IPIP-50 responses, we analyze geometry on SPD manifolds under manipulated question orderings in GPT-4o simulating American and Chinese-American personas. We find that persona expression comprises two dissociable components: aggregated features (Big Five scores) degrade under randomization (21% drop) but are frame-robust; geometric features (SPD manifold) collapse under frame misalignment (42% drop) but recover substantially (to 84%) under shared frames, surpassing aggregated features (76%). This collapse-recovery pattern reveals that persona geometry is not intrinsic but a frame-dependent coordination pattern encoding information invisible to aggregation. Our findings establish a dual-nature framework for LLM personas, frame-dependent geometry versus frame-robust aggregates, necessitating frame-aware evaluation and challenging static trait conceptions.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4o express 'personas'—consistent behavioral patterns—when answering psychometric questionnaires. It finds that LLMs' personas have two parts: one that reflects broad personality traits (like the 'Big Five' traits) and another that depends on the framing of questions. When question order is randomized, the broad traits degrade, but the frame-dependent part remains stable.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work reveals how LLMs can dynamically adapt their outputs based on input framing, signaling potential challenges for regulators in ensuring consistent and predictable behavior from AI systems in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: LLMs may exhibit context-dependent behavior, complicating efforts to regulate their market impact or ensure fair competition in AI-driven services.

items.title: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces **SkillFuzz**, a tool to detect **implicit intents**—unintended objectives that emerge when multiple individually benign skills (reusable software components for AI agents) interact in an **open skill marketplace** (a platform where users assemble AI agents from community-contributed skills). The authors argue that marketplace operators currently audit skills in isolation, missing risks that only arise from skill composition.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights systemic risks in open skill marketplaces that could enable anti-competitive behavior or consumer harm through unchecked skill interactions, signaling the need for platform-level oversight akin to gatekeeper obligations under the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA).
_analysis.market_signal: Open skill marketplaces may become critical infrastructure for AI agents, raising concerns about platform accountability and the potential for implicit intents to undermine trust in AI-driven automation.

items.title: Facility Location Game with Envy Ratio
items.abstract: We study the one-facility location game on a real line with a new objective called envy ratio. The envy ratio, which is adopted from fair division and represents the egalitarianism, is defined as the maximum over the ratios between any two agents' utilities. We are interested in strategyproof or group strategyproof mechanisms that can minimize the envy ratio objective. We consider the model in two settings that can capture natural scenarios: the facility location and all the agents' locations are restricted on a fixed interval; every agent's location can be any point on the real line but the facility location is restricted on a relative interval. In both settings, we obtain the optimal solution and the best deterministic strategyproof mechanism which is also group strategyproof. In the first setting, we provide a lower bound for randomized strategyproof mechanisms. In the second setting, we give a lower bound and two upper bounds for randomized strategyproof mechanisms.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines a mathematical model called the 'facility location game' where agents (e.g., users or firms) compete to place a single facility (e.g., a data center, warehouse, or service) on a real line. The authors introduce a new fairness metric called the 'envy ratio' (the maximum ratio of utilities between any two agents), aiming to minimize this ratio to ensure egalitarian outcomes. They explore whether mechanisms exist that prevent agents from manipulating the outcome (strategyproofness) while achieving this fairness goal.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on a theoretical fairness metric in facility location, it indirectly relates to digital competition by modeling how platforms or firms might strategically place services (e.g., cloud data centers, AI model hubs) to avoid unfair advantages or consumer harm.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing interest in fairness and egalitarian principles in digital infrastructure placement, which could influence debates on equitable access to cloud services or AI resources.

items.title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
items.abstract: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces an autonomous research pipeline that uses large language models (LLMs) to analyze 11,083 physics papers and generate publication-grade manuscripts. Unlike previous AI agents that rely on internal calibration, this system cross-checks results against external literature to avoid hallucinations (AI-generated false but plausible outputs). The authors focus on improving reliability in frontier computational physics, where tools and methods are often poorly documented.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI agents can autonomously generate and validate scientific research, signaling potential disruption to knowledge-intensive markets and the role of gatekeepers in validating expertise.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven research automation could reduce reliance on traditional academic gatekeepers (e.g., peer review, journals), enabling new entrants to compete in knowledge production markets.

items.title: Constrained Distributed Heterogeneous Two-Facility Location Problems with Max-Variant Cost
items.abstract: This paper investigates a constrained distributed heterogeneous two-facility location problem under the max-variant cost model. In this setting, a set of agents with private locations on the real line is partitioned into disjoint groups. The constraint stipulates that facilities must be situated within a given multiset of candidate locations, with the restriction that each candidate location can host at most one facility. Under the max-variant model, an agent's individual cost is defined as the distance from their location to the farthest facility. Our objective is to design strategyproof distributed mechanisms that incentivize agents to report their locations truthfully while approximating social objectives. Such mechanisms operate in two stages: first, for each group, a pair of candidate locations is selected as representatives based solely on local reports; subsequently, the mechanism outputs two final facility locations from the set of all representatives. We focus on a class of deterministic strategyproof distributed mechanisms and establish constant lower and upper bounds on the distortion under four social objectives: Average-of-Average, Max-of-Max, Average-of-Max, and Max-o

_analysis.summary: This paper studies a mathematical problem about placing two facilities (e.g., data centers, warehouses, or service points) in optimal locations to minimize the maximum distance any user (e.g., customer, agent) has to travel, under constraints like limited candidate sites and group-specific rules. It focuses on a 'max-variant cost model,' where the cost for each user is determined by the farthest facility from their location.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper is purely mathematical and does not address digital markets directly, its core problem—constrained facility location with max-cost—mirrors real-world challenges in digital infrastructure (e.g., cloud computing, edge computing, or CDN placement), which are critical for platform competition and data center monopolies.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals growing academic interest in optimization problems that underpin digital infrastructure siting, which could indirectly inform antitrust scrutiny of data center monopolies or cloud provider dominance.

items.title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 game

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new way to manage memory in long-horizon AI agents (software systems that make decisions over extended periods) by using a 'bounded contract' that retrieves only relevant past interactions instead of storing all prior context. This avoids the problem of bloated, unmanageable prompts while preserving decision-making quality.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how AI agents could reduce reliance on dominant platforms' data and APIs by efficiently retrieving only necessary information, potentially disrupting data moats and platform control over user interactions.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with efficient memory retrieval may weaken the competitive advantages of platforms that hoard user interaction data (e.g., Google, Meta) by enabling third-party agents to operate independently.

items.title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
items.abstract: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supe

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Copewell, a multi-agent swarm system (a group of AI agents working together) designed to provide equitable mental wellness support, addressing gaps in global mental health treatment. It critiques existing single-mode AI wellness solutions for high abandonment rates and lack of personalized, immediate relief.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on mental health, the paper highlights the scalability and personalization potential of multi-agent AI systems, which could disrupt digital health markets and influence AI governance debates.
_analysis.market_signal: Multi-agent AI systems may drive demand for specialized AI infrastructure, reshaping competition in AI-as-a-service markets.

items.title: Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages
items.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines the growing use of large language models (LLMs) as evaluators ('LLM-as-a-Judge') for natural language tasks, particularly in multilingual and low-resource language settings where human validation is scarce. It highlights that LLMs often lack proficiency in these languages, raising reliability concerns for their use in academic and industry evaluations.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals how AI evaluation tools may introduce bias or unreliability in multilingual markets, indirectly affecting competition in AI-driven language services and content moderation.
